argument: Fifteen witnesses must read as one situated ecology before they read as fifteen controls. The offset bands, uneven scale, directional notches, and shared ground must carry the composition without interface chrome.

With labels, readout, controls, hint, and prose hidden, the first view must leave v045's slab, v046's vessel, and v047's proof strip. It should read as a field that can look back, not a flock illustration, tile grid, or dashboard.

The visitor must move through three different witnesses and look back. Pointer, touch, keyboard, and deterministic control paths must offer equivalent meaningful routes; no hover-only action may carry the work.
Proximity must turn an actual body toward the visitor. A moving cursor or halo is not reciprocal attention; the notch, facing edge, and directional trace must visibly answer presence.
One or two notices and repeated attention must remain geometry-neutral. Only three distinct witnesses can spend the stale direction and reorient the field.

Earlier Naive works protected the attended source while a remote target changed. v048 must break that invariant: a committed backcast changes the visited witnesses and every other agent through one global state.
A backcast must change geometry—orientation, notch depth, proportion, position, and stance—not only hue, opacity, or readout. The seam must be a consequence of the same field rule, not an annotation.
Four backcasts must compound in one ecology. Lift must reconstruct the exact preceding field and release must return to the deterministic quiet state.

Generated Canvas 2D directional bodies, live facing, consensus seams, and deterministic state are the medium. No screenshot, imported illustration, external font, animal drawing, or particle library may carry the work.

little-critters is translated from situated proximity and reciprocal looking into abstract witnesses and stale social consensus. Animals, eyes, characters, paper scene, source palette, source composition, source code, examples, and API surface are refused.
